overview: The file concerns postwar air communications between Japan and Korea, beginning with 1946 proposals by Transcontinental & Western Air and Asia Airways to establish American-controlled commercial services during the Allied occupation of Japan. Asia Airways’ detailed prospectus links civil aviation to Japan’s transportation shortages, economic recovery, demilitarization, American strategic influence, and intelligence interests. Most of the file documents a 1949 dispute over CINCFE’s termination of scheduled military flights between Japan and Gimpo near Seoul: Ambassador John J. Muccio argued that commercial Northwest Airlines service could not adequately carry official mail, personnel, supplies, newspapers, and recreational material, while CINCFE denied any continuing obligation to provide routine military transport. State Department intervention led toward restoration of a weekly, non-reimbursable courier flight, with later discussion of its budgetary future; a final, somewhat tangential airgram concerns proposed CNAC operating or landing rights.

subfiles.title: Symington transmits airline applications for Japan–Korea service
subfiles.from: W. Stuart Symington, Assistant Secretary of War for Air
subfiles.about: Symington forwards applications from Transcontinental & Western Air and Asia Airways for authority to operate air services in Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: General MacArthur had determined that existing military transport was adequate for occupation requirements, so the applications could not be justified solely by military necessity. Symington recommends that applications from American or other United Nations carriers be considered under a general national policy then being studied by the State Department and Air Coordinating Committee.

subfiles.title: TWA proposal for operations in Japan and Korea
subfiles.about: TWA offers to establish internal Japanese and Korean routes and a Japan–Korea service under military contract, with possible later conversion to commercial operation.
subfiles.summary: TWA emphasizes its financial resources, two decades of experience, Civil Aeronautics Board certificates, and wartime contract work for the Army. It proposes using Army airports and facilities under the direction of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers. Once permitted, the contract operation could become a scheduled commercial service carrying Japanese and other fare-paying passengers under occupation priorities and regulations.

subfiles.title: Asia Airways application letter
subfiles.from: Ernest J. Silver, President, Asia Airways
subfiles.to: W. Stuart Symington, Assistant Secretary of War for Air
subfiles.about: Asia Airways requests consideration of its application to begin operating in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Silver encloses the company prospectus and asks that it be retained if immediate consideration is premature. He notes that an application was already pending with General Headquarters of the Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers in Tokyo and that GHQ had advised applying to Symington’s office as well.

subfiles.title: Asia Airways prospectus and route maps
subfiles.about: The prospectus presents an operational, financial, staffing, and strategic plan for an American-controlled airline serving Japan and neighboring Asian destinations.
subfiles.summary: Asia Airways proposes daily C-47 service among Fukuoka, Osaka, Tokyo, and Sapporo, initially with four aircraft and a Tokyo-area maintenance base. It argues that wartime damage, coal shortages, slow rail journeys, inadequate ferries, and the loss of coastal shipping created demand for rapid passenger, mail, document, news-film, and express transport. The company couples economic-recovery arguments with occupation aims: flight and maintenance work would remain in American hands, while Japanese personnel would be confined mainly to traffic, sales, meteorology, communications, and office work. The plan calls for 137 employees, $300,000 in capital, fares of fifty sen per kilometer, possible government mail revenue, and feeder connections with Korean National Airways and a certified U.S. trans-Pacific carrier; accompanying maps depict proposed routes and expansion toward Manila and Taihoku, now Taipei.

subfiles.title: Muccio protests termination of Japan–Gimpo airlift
subfiles.about: Muccio protests the abrupt end of scheduled military flights from Japan to Gimpo and requests restoration of at least one weekly military flight.
subfiles.summary: The September 7 termination is described as a heavy blow to the American Mission and KMAG and as inconsistent with the mission’s understanding of CINCFE’s logistical obligations. Muccio warns of delays to mail, personnel movement and leave, Armed Forces radio station WVTP, and motion-picture distribution. He proposes two weekly connections: one Northwest Airlines flight early in the week and one FEAF or MATS flight on Thursday or Friday.

subfiles.title: Second copy of Muccio telegram on airlift termination
subfiles.to: CINCFE; Department of the Army; Secretary of State
subfiles.about: A second, partly garbled transmission records Muccio’s objections to ending scheduled military airlift service between Japan and Gimpo.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats the argument that the Gimpo handover did not eliminate the need for twice-weekly courier connections and that Northwest Airlines’ existing schedule was inadequate. It lists delays to parcel post, personnel, leave travel, radio operations, and motion-picture service. The proposed solution is an early-week commercial flight supplemented by a Thursday or Friday FEAF or MATS flight.

subfiles.title: Acheson replies to Muccio on the airlift disruption
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the disruption caused by ending the Japan–Gimpo airlift and asks the embassy to report new arrangements or recommendations.
subfiles.summary: Acheson states that the Department shares the embassy’s concern about interrupted communications. The embassy is asked to keep Washington fully and promptly informed of any replacement arrangements and of further recommendations for meeting its needs.

subfiles.title: CINCFE rejects responsibility for a regular Korea airlift
subfiles.from: Commander in Chief, Far East, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Department of the Army; Seoul, Korea; Department of State
subfiles.about: CINCFE denies a continuing obligation to provide regularly scheduled military flights after relinquishing operational responsibility for Gimpo Air Base.
subfiles.summary: CINCFE reviews earlier directives and contends that none required scheduled air support after the withdrawal of its Gimpo detachment. Northwest Airlines had reportedly offered two weekly Tokyo–Seoul round trips, which CINCFE considered sufficient if the American Mission arranged expanded commercial service. CINCFE would provide emergency support but rejected routine military flights, especially for purposes not authorized for military aircraft or provided without reimbursement.

subfiles.title: Muccio requests State–Army intervention for weekly flight
subfiles.about: Muccio reports possible additional Northwest Airlines service but maintains that the mission and KMAG still require a weekly military aircraft.
subfiles.summary: An extra Friday or Saturday commercial flight would solve the urgent courier problem but not carry all parcel post, publications, emergency exchange supplies, or personnel formerly moved by military aircraft. Muccio argues that KMAG’s approximately 500 personnel alone justify a weekly flight from Japan. He asks the Department to approach the Department of the Army informally and seek instructions to CINCFE.

subfiles.title: Department announces restoration of weekly courier flight
subfiles.from: James E. Webb, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department reports that the National Military Establishment is acting to restore a weekly, non-reimbursable Tokyo–Seoul courier flight.
subfiles.summary: The message attributes the action to representations by the Acting Secretary of State. It indicates that a weekly courier service between Tokyo and Seoul should be reinstated promptly and without reimbursement.

subfiles.title: Reber memorandum on proposed letter restoring the airlift
subfiles.to: Mr. McWilliams; for signature by the Acting Secretary
subfiles.about: Reber summarizes a proposed high-level letter seeking immediate restoration of adequate military airlift between Japan and Korea.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that the September 7 termination violated a prior State–Military–ECA agreement for a daily, non-reimbursable C-46 round trip between Tokyo and Seoul. It quotes Muccio’s warning that the decision gravely damaged every part of the combined mission. The proposed letter offers further discussion but requests immediate action to meet the mission’s minimum needs.

subfiles.title: Deputy Under Secretary’s background memorandum on the airlift dispute
subfiles.from: Office of the Deputy Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The memorandum supplies background supporting an appeal to the Secretary of Defense over the termination of the Japan–Seoul airlift.
subfiles.summary: It explains that commercial transportation would not meet the mission’s needs and would require funds that were unavailable because the military service had been promised without reimbursement. The proposed letter had been cleared with Paul G. Hoffman and prepared with staff from Under Secretary of the Army Tracy S. Voorhees’s office. The memorandum also cites an earlier Air Force removal of ground-controlled-approach equipment from Gimpo and argues that negotiations over responsibility in Germany made enforcement of interdepartmental support commitments especially important.

subfiles.title: Muccio reiterates need for a Thursday military flight
subfiles.to: CINCFE; Department of State; Department of the Army
subfiles.about: Muccio welcomes twice-weekly Northwest Airlines service but again requests a weekly military flight, preferably on Thursday.
subfiles.summary: Muccio says that commercial service would help but could not satisfy the varied requirements of the mission, particularly those of the 500-person KMAG detachment. He asks for a fixed weekly military schedule and promises to arrange Korean government clearance once the schedule is established.

subfiles.title: Kimball memorandum on funding the Tokyo–Seoul airlift
subfiles.to: Record; copies to VanWagoner, Foster, Lawson, and Williams
subfiles.about: Kimball records discussions about whether non-reimbursable Tokyo–Seoul airlift service should end on June 30, 1950 and who should fund it thereafter.
subfiles.summary: Kimball told Army officers that the original arrangement contained no termination date and that future responsibility should be decided by the Bureau of the Budget. Mr. Lawson believed a decision should await congressional action on the Korean air program. The Army agreed to revisit whether later service would be reimbursable and to reiterate instructions that CINCFE restore non-reimbursable weekly service for the current fiscal year.

subfiles.title: Airgram concerning CNAC operating rights
subfiles.about: The airgram refers to embassy reporting on proposed CNAC operations, negotiations for operating or landing rights, and the airline president’s attitude toward the Chinese government.
subfiles.summary: The message cross-references embassy despatches of October 1 and October 7 for information about the carrier identified by OCR as “CHAC,” evidently CNAC. It notes negotiations involving the Chinese and French consuls and indicates that the company president’s relationship with the Chinese government could affect the outcome.

interest: The file is especially useful for showing how routine communications and transport became an interagency test of authority, funding, and military responsibility during the transition from occupation administration to commercial aviation. The Asia Airways prospectus is unusually candid in combining economic reconstruction with the exclusion of Japanese personnel from technical aviation, maintenance of an American reserve cadre, and potential intelligence collection. The two copies of Muccio’s September 15 telegram also permit comparison of transmission errors and bureaucratic circulation. Despite a catalog title mentioning carrier pigeons, the surviving documents concern aircraft, airline policy, and courier flights, illustrating the sometimes loose relationship between decimal-file headings and actual contents.
